lesson.title: Where a Graph Shoots to Infinity: Vertical Asymptotes
lesson.summary: A vertical asymptote occurs at x equals a exactly when a function's one-sided limit there is infinite, and for rational functions this happens precisely at zeros of the denominator that are not canceled by the numerator.
lesson.body:
A vertical asymptote is the precise, fixed-input version of the general asymptote idea just introduced. The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f if at least one of the one-sided limits there is infinite: the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left equals positive or negative infinity, or the limit as x approaches a from the right equals positive or negative infinity. This is exactly the situation at an infinite discontinuity: a itself is not in the domain of f, and instead of settling to a finite value or being repairable by cancellation, the function's output diverges as x closes in on a.

For a rational function f(x) = p(x)/q(x) written in lowest terms, meaning any common factors between p and q have already been canceled, vertical asymptotes occur at exactly the real zeros of q(x). This connects directly back to the continuity of rational functions: at a zero a of the denominator, the function is necessarily discontinuous, and that discontinuity is infinite, producing a vertical asymptote, precisely when p(a) is not zero. When p(a) is also zero, the factor cancels and the discontinuity is removable instead, a hole rather than an asymptote.

Consider f(x) = (x + 2)/(x^2 - 4). Factoring the denominator gives x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2), so f(x) = (x + 2)/[(x - 2)(x + 2)]. For every x other than -2, the factor (x + 2) cancels top and bottom, leaving f(x) = 1/(x - 2). At x = -2, both the original numerator and denominator equal 0, so this is a removable discontinuity, a hole in the graph, not an asymptote. At x = 2, only the denominator is zero, since the numerator x + 2 evaluated at x = 2 equals 4, which is nonzero. So x = 2 is a genuine vertical asymptote.

Checking the one-sided limits at x = 2 directly confirms this using the simplified form 1/(x - 2). As x approaches 2 from the right, for instance x = 2.01, the quantity x - 2 is a small positive number, so 1/(x - 2) is a large positive number, giving a limit of positive infinity. As x approaches 2 from the left, for instance x = 1.99, x - 2 is a small negative number, so 1/(x - 2) is a large negative number, giving a limit of negative infinity. Since at least one, in fact both, of the one-sided limits is infinite, x = 2 is confirmed as a vertical asymptote.

The general test, then, is to factor numerator and denominator fully, cancel any shared factors first, and check the zeros of what remains in the denominator: those surviving zeros are vertical asymptotes, while any canceled zero is a removable hole instead. This same reasoning extends beyond rational functions to any quotient of continuous pieces. The tangent function, tan x = sin x / cos x, has a vertical asymptote at x = pi/2 by identical logic, since cos(pi/2) = 0 while sin(pi/2) = 1 is nonzero, so no cancellation rescues the discontinuity there.
